title: Vetala Extended Tale 28: The Faithful Horse and the Ungrateful Master

full_text:
Night deepened as King Vikramaditya walked steadfastly through the thorny briars of the burning ground. The Vetala resumed his tale.

"Listen, Vikramaditya, to the story of the merchant Dhanapala and his noble steed, Pawan. In his youth, Pawan had saved Dhanapala from ruthless bandits, carrying him out of an ambush despite taking an arrow to its flank. For fifteen years, the horse carried Dhanapala's merchandise across treacherous mountain passes, making the merchant wealthy beyond measure.

Yet when Pawan grew old, lame, and gray, Dhanapala refused to spend grain on an animal that could no longer work. He drove the faithful creature out into the scorching streets to scavenge dry leaves and refuse. The townspeople saw the famished horse stumbling near the temple bell, but none took it in, each saying, 'It is not our responsibility; it belongs to the rich merchant.'

One afternoon, the starving horse stumbled against the temple bell-rope, ringing the bell of justice. The king of that land summoned the town council.

Tell me, Vikram," demanded the Vetala, "who incurred the greatest guilt under dharma: Dhanapala who abandoned his savior, or the citizens who turned away their eyes?"

King Vikramaditya replied: "Dhanapala bore the greatest guilt by far. The citizens were guilty of indifference, but Dhanapala had entered into a sacred bond of gratitude and debt. Pawan had bled for him and built his fortune. To discard a faithful protector the moment his utility ends is the highest betrayal of trust and dharma."

"True to your fame!" cried the Vetala, and with a cackle, he soared back to the shimshepa bough.
moral: Betraying those who served you with unwavering devotion in your time of weakness is the darkest stain on human honor.
